summaries.example: Imagine a logic game. The opponent says, “You are in Rome,” even though everyone knows you are not. The respondent must first accept that sentence for the game. If the opponent then says, “You are in Rome or you are a bishop,” the respondent accepts it because it is true. If the opponent next says, “You are a bishop,” the respondent may also have to accept it because that sentence follows from the earlier answers in the game. The point is not to pretend the person is really a bishop. The point is to follow the rules without contradicting accepted answers.
summaries.summary: Obligationes were medieval rules for handling a special kind of logical disputation. Two people took part: an opponent offered sentences, and a respondent accepted or rejected them. In the common form, called positio, the respondent had to accept a false sentence at the start. After that, the respondent still had to respect logical connections. Sentences that followed from the starting sentence were accepted, and sentences that conflicted with it were rejected. Unconnected sentences were judged on their own. Medieval authors disagreed about how earlier answers should affect later ones. Walter Burley’s influential approach treated the order of the exchange as important and aimed at a coherent set of answers. Richard Kilvington proposed thinking about what would be true if the false starting sentence were true. Roger Swyneshed developed rules that could permit some larger groups of answers to conflict. These theories show that the medieval study was about keeping track of logical relationships, not simply labeling every sentence true or false.
key_ideas: Medieval thinkers studied arguments as organized question-and-answer games.
In the usual game, a person had to accept a false starting sentence but still answer in a logically orderly way.
A sentence that follows from the starting sentence had to be accepted; one that conflicts with it had to be rejected.
A sentence with no connection was judged by whether it was true or false on its own.
Different thinkers changed the rules, especially about whether the order of sentences mattered.
summaries.why_it_matters: These theories show that logic can study how commitments change during a conversation. They also show that a debate can have rules about coherence even when it begins with a false assumption. This connects medieval logic with questions people still ask about arguments, dialogue, consistency, and what follows from what.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking about whether statements support, conflict with, or have no connection to one another.
A special duty in a medieval logic game. It told the respondent what sentence to accept, reject, or sometimes question.
The starting sentence that the respondent had to accept in the most common kind of game, even when it was false.
A statement that has a logical connection to the starting sentence or to answers already given.

summaries.example: Consider a disputation with the starting positum “You are in Rome,” accepted as possible even though the respondent is not in Rome. The next proposition is “You are not in Rome or you are a bishop.” Burley’s standard theory treats this as irrelevant at that stage and grants it because it is true. The next proposition, “You are a bishop,” is then relevant: together with the earlier granted disjunction, it is treated as following from the developing set of answers, so it must be granted. This illustrates Burley’s striking conclusion that, with a false contingent positum, many false propositions compatible with it can eventually be forced into the answer sequence. Kilvington rejects this result
summaries.summary: Medieval obligationes were formal theories of how a respondent should manage commitments in a disputation. The opponent presented propositions in sequence, while the respondent normally granted or denied them. In positio, the respondent began by accepting a specified proposition, commonly an obviously false one. This exceptional acceptance suspended the ordinary requirement to follow truth at every step, but it did not suspend the requirement to avoid certain logical failures. Walter Burley’s influential rules required granting the positum, granting propositions that followed from it, denying propositions incompatible with it, and responding to irrelevant propositions according to their own truth-status. Burley also made relevance depend on previous answers, so the sequence could expand the set of propositions that had to be treated as connected. Richard Kilvington objected that this could force the respondent to grant arbitrary falsities. His counterfactual proposal evaluated claims according to what would be true if the positum were true, making order less important. Roger Swyneshed also rejected Burley’s order dependence, but without adopting the same counterfactual method; his rules could produce certain contradictory triads. Thus, the theories disagree over what coherent commitment requires. The entry presents obligationes as a study of dynamic logical relations within an evolving sequence, not merely as ordinary true-or-false classification.
key_ideas: Obligationes focus on the logical duty of coherence rather than on ordinary truth-telling alone.
In Burley’s standard theory, the respondent must grant the positum, grant what follows from it, deny what is incompatible with it, and judge irrelevant propositions by their own truth or falsity.
Burley’s rules use the history and order of earlier answers: an initially irrelevant proposition can help make a later proposition relevant.
Kilvington and an anonymous author proposed a counterfactual alternative in which answers depend on what would be true if the positum were true, not on the order of presentation.
Swyneshed rejected Burley’s key order-sensitive rules in another way, allowing some contradictory triads while still preserving special restrictions concerning the positum.
The mainstream later view is often interpreted as a dynamic attempt to maintain logical coherence, although the competing theories show that this interpretation is not complete for every author.
summaries.why_it_matters: Obligationes provide an early, technically detailed study of reasoning in dialogue. They separate truth from what a participant is required to grant within a rule-governed context, a distinction important for analyzing assumptions, inferences, and commitments. Their competing theories also raise enduring questions about consistency, counterfactual reasoning, the effect of conversational order, and whether a logical game represents a possible situation or only relations among propositions.

important_terms.definition: A medieval branch of logic that analyzed duties for responding coherently in a structured disputation.
A disputation in which one participant presents propositions and another gives regulated evaluations, usually granting or denying them.
The standard obligation in which a proposition is laid down and must continue to be granted when presented.
A proposition that follows from, or is incompatible with, the obligation or with the developing answers; it therefore receives a rule-governed response.
A logical relation in which one proposition is supported by another proposition or group of propositions.
The requirement that answers fit together without the kind of conflict found in a contradictory set; the medieval authors did not always use this modern vocabulary explicitly.
Reasoning about what would be true if a proposition were accepted as the case, even though it is not actually true.
A theory associated with Roger Swyneshed that rejects some of Burley’s order-sensitive rules and can require acceptance of certain incompatible groups of propositions.

questions_to_think_about: Is Burley’s order-sensitive method a good account of coherence, or does it allow too many conclusions from a false positum?
What is gained and lost when a disputation is interpreted counterfactually?
Can a system be logically interesting if some of its permitted answers form a contradiction?
Why might medieval authors distinguish what must be granted from what is simply true?
Does a sequence of answers describe a possible situation, or does it merely display changing logical relations among propositions?

summaries.summary: Medieval theories of obligationes studied how a person should answer in a carefully controlled disputation. The opponent introduced propositions one at a time, and the respondent usually granted or denied them. In the most commonly discussed form, positio, the opponent required acceptance of a false starting proposition. The respondent was not expected to treat that proposition as an ordinary fact, but was expected to avoid violating the logical rules of the exchange. Burley’s standard theory divided later propositions into relevant and irrelevant ones. Relevant propositions were those that followed from, or were incompatible with, the positum and the answers already given. They had to be granted or denied accordingly. An irrelevant proposition was judged by its own truth or falsity. Because earlier answers could make later claims relevant, the order of the exchange mattered. Other medieval logicians challenged this system. Kilvington argued that the respondent should answer according to what would be true if the positum were true, rather than being pushed into accepting any false claim that happened to become relevant. Swyneshed also rejected Burley’s order-based rules, but his alternative could permit certain contradictory sets of answers. The wider tradition therefore explored several accounts of logical commitment, coherence, and consequence.
key_ideas: The usual obligation game begins with an agreed special assumption, often a false one.
The respondent’s task is not simply to report reality; it is to manage the logical consequences of the assumption.
Burley made relevance depend partly on answers given earlier, so the order of the opponent’s claims matters.
Kilvington and an anonymous writer proposed a counterfactual method that reduces the importance of order.
Swyneshed rejected Burley differently and allowed some combinations of answers that seem contradictory.
The theories grew out of ancient and medieval work on dialectical questioning, impossible assumptions, and logical consequence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Obligationes help explain how arguments work when people reason from assumptions that they do not ordinarily believe. They distinguish a claim’s truth from what a speaker must say within a formal dialogue. Studying the disagreements also teaches that logical systems can share a goal—coherent reasoning—while disagreeing about the rules that best achieve it.

important_terms.definition: A medieval form of logic about how to respond correctly in a structured exchange of propositions.
A formal conversation in which one person presents claims and another must evaluate them according to rules.
The initial claim that the respondent is required to accept in the main type of obligation game, even if it is false.
A claim that follows from, or conflicts with, the starting claim or with the growing set of accepted information.
A claim with no logical connection to the obligation at that point; it is judged by its own truth or falsity.
A statement or group of statements that logically supports another statement.
A proposal to answer as things would be if the false starting claim were true.
A set of answers that does not contain the kinds of logical conflicts that make the answers pull against one another.
